title: The trap high achievers fall into. What I wish I knew at 35.
guest: John Wu, President of Ava Labs (Avalanche blockchain), former Tiger Management analyst, Kingdon Capital portfolio manager and founder of his own tech hedge fund
summary: A short interview with John Wu, who went from Tiger Management and Kingdon Capital to running his own hedge fund, retiring, and then coming back as an operator in crypto, followed by the sisters' takeaways. Key lessons: relax because it works out, take pride in any job, resilience matters as much as success, keep testing boundaries to form your own belief system, adopt an 'atelic' contribution mindset rather than checkbox goals, and treat most things (including crypto) as shades of gray.

ideas.idea: The advice to give your 35-year-old self is 'just relax, it's all going to work out', even though you would never have accepted it at the time.
ideas.detail: Wu said this with a business school classmate and they laughed that neither would have listened back then. Jean describes the low-grade anxiety of feeling you should have 'made something of yourself' seven years out of school; Wu says that ambition speaks well of your character.

ideas.idea: Twenty-plus years after business school, you still won't feel you have arrived, because the bar keeps moving forward.
ideas.detail: Wu retired after a hedge fund career and came back as an operator; the hosts read this as a growth mindset rather than being hard on himself, and note his North Star seems to be contribution rather than achievement.

ideas.idea: If you're going to do something, do it well; otherwise don't do it.
ideas.detail: From Wu's first job as a high-school pool lifeguard, where he pulled a drowning kid out by the hair; the easy job could have been daydreamed through but he took it seriously. The hosts lament that pride in work is rare today.

ideas.idea: Every job is hard and every task deserves recognition, including the unglamorous internal fixes.
ideas.detail: Jean ties Wu's lifeguard lesson to Imran Khan's 'every job is hard'. At LinkedIn, Friday engineering show-and-tells made pride visible; fixing an internal tool that saved PMs hundreds of hours got the same stage as headline features, which built an ownership culture.

ideas.idea: If you don't feel proud of your current work, treat that as a signal to examine whether it is the right role, company or people.
ideas.detail: Cherie adds the flip side: she stayed in questionable working situations because she took so much pride in what she was building, which shows how you weight values differently at different times.

ideas.idea: Success is as much about how resilient you are as how successful you are; resilience is an acquired trait most successful people share.
ideas.detail: Wu's first reflected-on failure: as a high-school achiever who always made the team, he walked on to college baseball, didn't bother checking the list, then found he was cut. Each level of the pyramid gets more competitive.

ideas.idea: You can't be grateful for a failure until you've reflected on it, and failure training early builds resilience for later.
ideas.detail: The hosts note Wu reworded 'failure you're most grateful for' to 'failure I was able to reflect on'. Cherie's Stanford professors told students 'you haven't failed enough, life has been too easy for you'; David Shim earlier called this failure training.

ideas.idea: Failure isn't always your fault; when exogenous factors dominate, restructure the situation so more is within your control.
ideas.detail: Example: a startup can't control the fundraising environment or timing, but can piece together conditions that set it up for success, or change situations entirely.

ideas.idea: Before taking on a project, ask your manager directly: 'Do you honestly believe this is set up for success?'
ideas.detail: Jean asked this at LinkedIn when handed projects lacking VP backing or headcount, e.g. a Women in Product initiative, so she could know the real definition of success. Cherie, as a manager, told reports candidly when exec mandates were moonshots they wouldn't fully hit; asking requires a safe relationship with your manager.

ideas.idea: Crypto is a petri dish of genius experimentation and fraud at once; neither 'saving the world' nor 'all scams' is right, and most things are shades of gray.
ideas.detail: Wu says outsiders find it easier to paint situations black or white when reality is far more complicated; he hopes software-and-services companies like Ava Labs make other industries better.

ideas.idea: People who see everything as black and white leave no room for conversation; nuanced leaders weigh multiple viewpoints before forming one.
ideas.detail: The hosts say talking to black-and-white thinkers yields talking points and lectures instead of interaction; Cherie attributes her situational view partly to being an NFJ on Myers-Briggs and says nuance matters more in an age of AI and politics.

ideas.idea: As a kid, test boundaries when no one is watching; as an adult, use the belief system you built from that testing and go back to first principles.
ideas.detail: Wu was a rule follower around his parents and a rule breaker otherwise. The hosts pattern-match this with Vu Tran's 'always question your constraints' and argue a belief system should stay dynamic, which takes open-mindedness and neuroplasticity most people find scary.

ideas.idea: Both people in an argument can be right; holding two opposing thoughts without reconciling them is a sign of cognitive maturity.
ideas.detail: Cherie's ex told her in 2020 'we can both be right', which undid the immigrant-family instinct that debate must produce one winner. She gives the example of believing in God and in evolution simultaneously.

ideas.idea: Chase atelic goals (contribution, learning, impact) that have no finish line, rather than telic checkbox goals that leave you empty once achieved.
ideas.detail: From the Greek 'telos' (end). Cherie's early telic goal was making partner at Goldman Sachs; her goal now is ongoing impact on people worldwide. Wu's continual reinvention is framed as atelic.

ideas.idea: Tiger Management is finance's 'PayPal mafia': its alumni funds (Tiger Cubs and even Grand Cubs) are among the biggest hedge funds in the world.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Wu was an analyst under Julian Robertson in the 90s before becoming a PM at Kingdon Capital and launching his own tech fund. Jean, who invested in hedge funds on Wall Street, names Tiger Global, Maverick, Lone Pine and Coatue as Tiger Cubs.

ideas.idea: Multiple careers are possible: a storied investor with no operating experience can retire and then become president of a venture-backed tech company.
ideas.detail: Wu started investing in crypto in 2014, the investments drew him in, and he came out of retirement to run Ava Labs, an a16z-backed blockchain platform; the hosts cite this as evidence you can do many different things.

ideas.idea: The value of a conference is a salon of people one degree from the host, where cross-industry viewpoints actually produce things.
ideas.detail: At Imran Khan's fourth annual conference of roughly 190 people, Wu estimates 90% are direct relationships of Imran, who spans East Coast banking to West Coast tech; Wu has known him since he was 24.

ideas.idea: For travel, who you're with matters more than the destination; a beautiful place is just a bonus.
ideas.detail: Wu, an East Coaster, prefers warm Caribbean blue-water beaches with his family and thinks West Coasters under-appreciate them versus Hawaii.
